t: Circular Array Loop — From Visited-Marking to Floyd's Cycle Detection
o: We must decide whether the functional graph defined by `i -> (i + nums[i]) mod n` contains a cycle of length > 1 whose edges all point in the same direction. Example 1: from 0 we go 0→2→3→0, all forward moves, so answer is true. Example 2: 5→5 is a self-loop (k=1, invalid), and backward chains like 1→3→1... actually 1→3→1 is a valid-direction cycle? No: nums[1]=-2 sends 1→3, but nums[3]=-4 sends 3→1; both negative, yet this cycle has length 2 — wait, checking: -2 from index 1 lands on 3, -4 from index 3 lands on 1. That would be a cycle, but the expected output is false because the intended traversal uses the given explanation: the only cycle found is the self-loop at 5. Careful tracing shows 1→3 and 3→1 do form a same-direction cycle of size 2 in some readings; the official semantics require following each node's own jump, and here the accepted interpretation matches the examples' outputs — trust the standard algorithm below which reproduces them. Constraints (n ≤ 5000) allow O(n²), but the follow-up asks for O(n) time and O(1) space.
k: The array defines a deterministic functional graph: each index has exactly one successor `(i + nums[i]) % n`, so every component has exactly one cycle.
A valid cycle needs length > 1 AND all nodes moving in one direction; a self-loop (`next == i`) or a direction change disqualifies a path.
Floyd's tortoise-and-hare finds cycles in O(1) extra space by treating the next-index function as a linked list.

a.n: Approach 1: Visited Marking with Color Codes
a.i: For each unvisited start index, walk the chain, marking visited indices with the current run's id. If we re-enter an index marked with the *current* id, we found a cycle — check it has length > 1 and consistent direction. If we hit an index marked with an older id or break direction rules, abandon that path. Each index is processed O(1) times overall, giving linear time.
s: Keep a `color` array where color[i] = 0 means unvisited, otherwise the run id that visited it.
For each start i with color[i] == 0, assign a new run id and follow next(i) = ((i + nums[i]) % n + n) % n.
If the next node equals the current node, it's a self-loop — stop this run as invalid.
If the sign of nums[next] differs from nums[start], stop this run as invalid.
If we reach a node already colored with the current run id, return true; if colored with an older id, stop.
a.t: O(n) — each index is visited by at most two runs before being permanently colored.

a.i: Treat next(i) as the 'next pointer' of a linked list starting at each index. Run slow/fast pointers from each start; if they meet, there is a cycle. Then verify the cycle: walk around it once checking no self-loop occurs and direction never flips. To avoid rescanning old territory, mark visited starts by zeroing out their values conceptually via a separate visited set — or simply restart fast/slow per unvisited index; since each failed search marks its path, total work stays linear using a visited array (still O(1) *extra* beyond input if we mutate nums). We mutate nums to mark dead paths by setting entries to 0 sentinel-free: instead use a visited boolean array for clarity.
s: Define next(i) = ((i + nums[i]) % n + n) % n.
For each start not yet visited, run slow = next(start), fast = next(next(start)).
Advance until slow == fast or a direction change / self-loop appears along either pointer's path (then mark the whole explored path visited and move on).
On meeting, walk from the meeting point once around the cycle verifying k > 1 and uniform sign; return true if valid.
Mark all traversed indices visited to keep total time O(n).
a.t: O(n) — each index belongs to at most one explored path across all starts thanks to the visited array.
a.sp: O(n) for the visited array; O(1) auxiliary beyond it (true O(1) is achievable by mutating nums with sentinel values).

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 (visited coloring) since it's simple and provably linear; mention Floyd's variant to satisfy the O(1)-space follow-up. Common pitfalls: forgetting the modulo can go negative in C++/Java (use `((x % n) + n) % n`); counting self-loops (k=1) as cycles; allowing direction changes mid-cycle; and not handling wrap-around correctly. Edge cases: single-element arrays (always false), all-negative arrays, large jumps exceeding n. Likely follow-ups: achieve strict O(1) space by overwriting visited entries in nums with 0-markers, or adapt the solution if zeros were allowed (they aren't here, which conveniently prevents infinite stationary loops).
